title: Polynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut
formal:
Does undirected Edge Multiway Cut, parameterized only by the allowed number \(k\) of edge deletions, admit a randomized polynomial kernel? Specifically, do there exist a uniform randomized algorithm \(R\) and positive integers \(C,a,b\) such that for every explicitly encoded instance \(I=(G,T,k)\) of length \(N\), on every random tape \(R\) halts within \(C(N+1)^a\) steps and outputs a well-formed instance \(I'=(G',T',k')\) of the same problem with
\[|I'|\le C(k+1)^b,\qquad k'\le C(k+1)^b,\]
and
\[\Pr_R[I\text{ is a yes-instance}\ \Longleftrightarrow\ I'\text{ is a yes-instance}]\ge2/3?\]
A yes-instance has a set of at most \(k\) edges whose removal leaves no connected component containing two terminals. The number of terminals is unbounded and is not an extra parameter. The constants, including the exponent \(b\), must be independent of \(|T|\).
why: Kernelization asks whether the information relevant to a small cut budget can be compressed before solving the remaining hard instance. Edge Multiway Cut is a central test of that principle because it combines many terminal-separation requirements while parameterizing only the number of removed edges. A polynomial kernel would replace arbitrarily large graphs by uniformly small equivalent instances without fixing the number of terminals.

progress.text: Kratsch and Wahlström obtain polynomial kernels for Multiway Cut with a fixed number of terminals; the 2021 source states the dependence on that fixed number.

Wahlström’s revised full manuscript establishes randomized polynomial-time construction of quasipolynomial-size multicut-mimicking networks and, as a consequence, a randomized quasipolynomial Edge Multiway Cut kernel.
Gurjar and coauthors publish quasipolynomial-time derandomization of several matroid-based kernels, distinguishing those results from the unrestricted Edge Multiway Cut size question.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

sentences: Edge Multiway Cut removes a small number of edges so that no two designated terminals remain connected.
The question asks whether polynomial-time preprocessing can reduce any instance to an equivalent instance of size polynomial in the deletion budget alone.
The number of terminals is unrestricted, and the size exponent must not depend on it.
Randomized preprocessing is allowed with a per-instance equivalence guarantee of at least two thirds.
Known fixed-terminal kernels and quasipolynomial-size kernels leave the unrestricted polynomial-size target open in the checked sources.

definitions:
An input graph is a finite undirected unweighted loopless multigraph \(G=(V,E)\). Vertices are labeled \(1,\ldots,n\); edges are an explicitly listed sequence of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Parallel edges are distinct listed objects, each costing one deletion. The terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) consists of distinct designated vertices. The budget \(k\ge0\) is an integer in binary. Encode \(n\) in unary, the edge-list length and endpoints in a self-delimiting binary format, the terminal set as an \(n\)-bit membership vector, and \(k\) in self-delimiting binary. The total encoding length \(N\) includes every listed edge, vertex and terminal and the budget. The output uses the same format; succinct circuits, binary edge multiplicities and binary weights are not allowed.

A cut is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of edge identities with \(|F|\le k\). The graph \(G-F\) retains every vertex and terminal. It must contain no path between any two distinct terminals. Terminals cannot be deleted, and terminal labels carry no further pairing data: every terminal must be separated from every other. Disconnected graphs, empty graphs, zero budgets and fewer than two terminals are included. The kernel need only preserve the decision answer, not the optimum cut value or every terminal-partition cut. It may relabel vertices and change the terminal set and budget.

The multigraph convention permits the contractions used in kernelization. It does not change polynomial-kernel existence relative to explicit simple graphs: replacing every edge by its own two-edge path through a fresh nonterminal gives a simple graph of polynomial encoding size with the same minimum number of edge deletions needed to separate terminals. Either part of such a path can be deleted at unit cost, while deleting both never helps beyond deleting one.

Use a uniform multitape probabilistic Turing machine with independent fair random bits and one transition per time unit, charging for writing the output. There is no advice, oracle or separately provided preprocessing. Runtime, output-format and size guarantees hold on every random tape. The probability of preserving equivalence is at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input, with two-sided error permitted. This explicitly fixes the saved card's allowance of randomized preprocessing; deterministic or one-sided-error polynomial kernels also qualify. The failure probability is not averaged over a distribution of graphs.

A polynomial kernel has size bounded solely by a fixed polynomial in \(k\), even when the original graph and terminal set are much larger. A bound such as \(k^{|T|+1}\) does not satisfy this condition, since its exponent changes with the input. A size bound \(k^{\log^{O(1)}k}\) is quasipolynomial and is likewise insufficient. Both bounds use the full encoding length, not just the number of vertices while ignoring labels, edges or weights.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the randomized polynomial-kernel claim. A positive proof must provide the preprocessing algorithm and verify the all-tape polynomial runtime, output size and parameter bounds, and per-instance equivalence probability for arbitrary terminal sets. A negative proof must rule out every algorithm in this model. A kernel for a fixed number of terminals, a reduction to a different decision language, quasipolynomial preprocessing or output size, or a conditional exclusion relying on an unproved complexity assumption does not by itself settle the stated unconditional claim.

context_blocks.text: The source contrasts polynomial kernels for each fixed terminal count with the open case of arbitrary terminal sets. For a bound \(|T|\le s\), the earlier kernel has a size exponent depending on \(s\); that dependence is exactly what the present question must avoid.

Wahlström proves a randomized quasipolynomial kernel for Edge Multiway Cut in the revised 2021 manuscript, with size \(k^{O(\log^3 k)}\) in the displayed bounds. The same work distinguishes a smaller nonconstructive mimicking-network bound from the network size achievable by randomized polynomial-time preprocessing.

The source’s mimicking networks preserve a richer family of terminal cut values. The benchmark asks only for an equivalent Edge Multiway Cut decision instance, so a solution does not need to construct such a stronger universal network.

The 2025 MFCS paper obtains deterministic kernels using quasipolynomial-time preprocessing for several problems whose randomized polynomial kernels were already known. It explicitly treats Multiway Cut with deletable terminals and separately mentions quasipolynomial-size Edge Multiway Cut kernels. Neither changing the deletion model nor allowing more preprocessing time resolves this card.
